title: Language That Deceives, Language That Creates. Why Can One Word Change Everything?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.
sources: Austin, John L., How to Do Things with Words, Oxford University Press 1962
Doukhan, Jacques B., Genesis, Seventh-day Adventist International Bible Commentary, Pacific Press 2016
Loftus, Elizabeth F., Leading Questions and the Eyewitness Report, “Cognitive Psychology” 7 (1975)
Loftus, Elizabeth F.; Palmer, John C., Reconstruction of Automobile Destruction: An Example of the Interaction between Language and Memory, “Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior” 13 (1974)

paragraphs: The American researcher Elizabeth Loftus once showed volunteers a film of two cars colliding and then asked them to estimate how fast the vehicles had been going. Those who were told at the outset that the cars had “contacted” each other gave an average of 40 km per hour. Participants whose question contained the word “smashed” put the speed at 50 km per hour. Although everyone had watched exactly the same film, their estimates differed by about 10 km per hour. The source of the difference was a single word: the leading question about cars that “smashed” assumed from the start that the collision was violent, and the human mind automatically adjusted to that frame.

The “innocent” question “You didn’t take out the trash again?” works in much the same way. The word “again” smuggles in a history of earlier failings, so the person being asked can only defend themselves. Linguists call this kind of hidden content presuppositions. An open statement is easy to challenge, because it is out in the open. But an assumption cleverly smuggled into a question slips past our critical thinking completely unchecked. Importantly, it takes no ill will to use words like these; most of the time, ordinary tiredness is enough.

Language, however, has another face as well. The philosopher John Langshaw Austin pointed out that words can change reality at the very moment they are spoken. Whoever says “I do” at the altar is, in that moment, getting married. A promise creates an obligation that did not exist a minute earlier, and the words “I’m sorry” and “I forgive you” change something between two people, even though nothing visible changes around them. Our world rests on sentences like these.

The Bible begins with a spoken word. In the first chapter of Genesis the divine voice sounds ten times, and each time it calls something new into being. The first words addressed to human beings are a blessing and a gift (Genesis 1:28-29). The third chapter, however, opens with a very different voice. The serpent begins with a question: “Did God really say, ‘You must not eat from any tree in the garden?’” (Genesis 3:1). In an instant he turns God’s generous assurance, “You may eat freely from every tree of the garden,” into a suggestion that God had forbidden them to eat from any tree at all. Then he waits for the woman to take up the discussion on his terms. The serpent does not order anyone to eat anything; he simply changes the way he portrays God and what God does. An honestly asked question leaves you free to choose, but the serpent’s words were nothing but a trap with a claim hidden inside.
Prepared by: Marek Micyk
Content editor: Beata Dutkowska

questions: What will my words create today?
challenge: Before you put down your phone or close your computer today, think of one question you asked someone in the last few days that was, at heart, a hidden accusation. Rephrase it honestly, without using the words “again” or “always.”

paragraphs: In the 1970s the American memory researcher Elizabeth Loftus carried out an experiment that changed the way we think about the human brain. She showed a group of volunteers a short film of a road accident: a car drives through an intersection, ignores a stop sign and hits another vehicle. The researchers then asked the participants to estimate the speed of the cars, deliberately changing a single word in the question. Some were asked how fast the cars were going when they “contacted” each other, while the others were asked about the moment they “smashed” into each other.

The results were surprising. Although everyone had watched exactly the same video, those who heard about cars that “smashed” estimated the speed at an average of 50 kilometers per hour. In the group asked about cars that “contacted”, the average was around 40 kilometers per hour. The real surprise, however, came in the second part of the study, carried out a week later. Asked whether they had seen any broken glass in the recording, participants from the “smashed” group said yes considerably more often, even though there was not a single shard in the film.

In another experiment the same psychologist asked forty people about their own experience of headaches. Participants whose questions suggested that the headaches were “frequent” reported an average of more than two a week. Those who were asked about “occasional” headaches mentioned fewer than one a week. That result gives pause, because the questions concerned their own bodies, a subject on which each of us considers ourselves an infallible expert.

A difference of ten kilometers per hour, the memory of glass that was never there, an extra headache every week: all of this was born of a single, seemingly unnoticeable word. A leading question about cars that “smashed” already carries a ready-made answer, because it assumes from the outset that the collision was violent. The human mind automatically adjusts to that frame before it has even had time to check the facts.
So if one word from a researcher can shift the boundaries of memory so dramatically, it is worth asking: how much power lies in the questions we fire at one another every day in our own homes?

sections.heading: A Question That Contains Its Answer
paragraphs: “You didn’t take out the trash again?” only looks like a question; in reality it is a verdict already passed. The word “again” smuggles in a whole history of earlier failings and immediately puts the other person on the defensive. The sentence “Why do you always have to be right?” works the same way. Nobody here is waiting for a reasoned explanation. The message assumes from the start that the other person pushes their opinion at any cost, and it forces them either to accept the charge or to fight it before they have even opened their mouth.

Linguists call hidden suggestions like these presuppositions. They are simply assumptions we have to accept as true for a statement to make sense at all. Our conversations are full of them every day, and under normal conditions they make life much easier. When you ask what time your sister is coming back, you assume that you have a sister, that she has gone out somewhere and that she plans to return, and the person you are talking to accepts all of this without batting an eye. But take a simple sentence like “When are you finally going to give me that money back?” and look at what lies beneath its surface. First: there is some money. Second: it belongs to the person asking. Third: someone borrowed it. Fourth: the time to pay it back has already come. Fifth: the borrower is dragging their feet. And sixth: the delay has gone on far too long.

Six assumptions in one short question, and not one of them stated outright. The real problem arises when one of these hidden pieces of information is false or hurtful, yet has been served up so innocently that no one registers it. An open statement is easy to challenge, because the message is out in the open. But an assumption cleverly smuggled into a question slips past our critical thinking completely unchecked.

This is how sensational headlines and advertising slogans work, but it is also how an ordinary person talks when they come home tired at the end of the day. It takes no ill will to ask a question with a hidden hook. A moment of carelessness is enough, and tiredness and emotion will write the rest of the script.

We fall into the trap of this kind of phrasing in our conversations with ourselves as well. The question “Why does this always happen to me?” looks like an attempt to understand the situation. In reality, though, it hides a ready-made and destructive claim: that bad luck is constantly pursuing us. Our mind, like an obedient detective, immediately starts gathering evidence to support the accusation. After a quarter of an hour of searching, we have a full case file of arguments in our head, though no one has even checked whether the charge itself is true. A completely different train of thought is set in motion by the question “What can I do about this tomorrow morning?” The starting situation remains exactly the same, but changing the linguistic frame radically changes the direction we take.

sections.heading: Sentences That Change Reality
paragraphs: Words, however, also have a second, entirely different face. In 1955 the Oxford philosopher John Langshaw Austin gave a series of lectures at Harvard University on sentences that have the power to transform reality at the very moment they are spoken. His ideas appeared in book form only after his death, under the telling title “How to Do Things with Words.”

Austin noticed that a person who says the solemn “I do” before the altar is not simply describing their emotional state: at that moment they are getting married. In the same way, someone who breaks a bottle of champagne against a ship’s hull while announcing its name ensures that from then on the vessel officially bears that name. A promise creates an obligation that did not exist even a minute earlier, whether or not it has been put down on paper. Phrases such as “I’m sorry” or “I forgive you” can instantly reshape a relationship between people, even though nothing around them has physically changed. Austin called these special utterances performatives. He also pointed out, however, that this remarkable power can misfire or be deliberately abused. A promise made lightly does not release the speaker from responsibility, because the other person immediately begins to build their plans on it. At this point the constructive power of language collides with its destructive shadow. Sometimes it is enough simply to utter the right sequence of words with nothing behind them.

Our social reality rests on declarations like these. Business contracts, weddings, loyalty in friendship and mutual trust at work are, at bottom, words that someone simply decided to turn into deeds. When we speak, we are designing the world in which other people will have to live. We can patiently build it up or systematically reduce it to ruins.

sections.heading: Ten Times “God Said”
paragraphs: In the first chapter of Genesis, boundless darkness and the primeval waters hang suspended, waiting for the first word. When it is finally spoken, it sets off a whole avalanche of change. The Creator speaks exactly ten times. God speaks and light is born; God speaks and dry land rises from the depths of the waters. According to Jewish tradition recorded in the Mishnah, in the tractate Pirkei Avot to be precise, the universe was called into being by ten divine utterances. Although individual rabbis count the verses in different ways, the final tally always remains the same.

The spoken words carry different kinds of power: they create new matter, separate light from darkness, give names to day and night, and every so often the approving summary returns that it was good. The first words addressed directly to human beings are especially interesting, because God first blesses them and then immediately gives them a gift: “Then God said, ‘Behold, I have given you every seed-bearing plant on the face of all the earth, and every tree whose fruit contains seed. They will be yours for food’” (Genesis 1:29). The second chapter brings a promise: the man receives complete freedom to eat from every tree in the garden, with just one clear exception (Genesis 2:16-17).

Then the Creator chooses to give human beings the ability to create new words. He brings the animals to the man to see what he will call them, and these human names become binding (Genesis 2:19). God, who created the world by His word, passes on to humanity a share of that same performative power.

The third chapter of Genesis opens with a completely different voice. The serpent, the most cunning of all the creatures the LORD God had made, begins with a question: “Did God really say, ‘You must not eat from any tree in the garden?’” (Genesis 3:1). Let us look at this closely. The serpent takes the two words that carry creative power, “God said”, and wraps them in two words that plant suspicion: “Did … really?” The generous “You may eat freely from every tree of the garden” becomes a ban on everything: “You must not eat from any tree in the garden.” At this stage the serpent is only asking, but he is using exactly the same trick as Loftus with her question about cars that “smashed”. He slips in a false picture of a stingy God and waits for the woman to start arguing within the frame he has imposed.

Eve corrects him and replies that they may eat the fruit of the trees of the garden. But the key word “every” disappears from her answer, and in its place appears a prohibition God never gave. She says they are not even allowed to touch the fruit (Genesis 3:2-3).

There is one more detail here, which the biblical scholar Jacques Doukhan points out. The narrator of the story consistently calls God “the LORD God”, a name that speaks of a close relationship with human beings. The serpent, however, calls Him only “God”. In the course of the conversation the woman quickly takes over his way of speaking. According to Doukhan, the fall began at precisely this moment, before anyone had even reached for the fruit: someone close and familiar had suddenly turned into a distant, impersonal concept.

Only now does the serpent openly assure her that they will certainly not die, and he adds that God knows full well that when they eat the fruit their eyes will be opened (Genesis 3:4-5). This is no longer a trick question but a direct attack on the Creator’s intentions, suggesting that He is keeping secrets from human beings. The next verse describes a change in the woman’s perception: suddenly she sees that the tree is good for food and pleasing to the eyes (Genesis 3:6). Yet that tree had stood there from the very beginning and looked exactly the same. All that had really changed were the words through which the woman had begun to look at it.

So the first temptation in the Bible comes as a purely linguistic maneuver. The serpent forces nothing and tells no one to eat the fruit. He simply reshapes the way people speak about God and leaves all the rest to human imagination.

sections.heading: Which Side Are Your Words On?
paragraphs: Scripture makes a surprising amount of room for asking questions. It is full of direct questions, and sometimes even angry ones. The psalmist cries out, “How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?” (Psalm 13:1), and these words have been written into the Bible for good. An honest question always leaves room for a real answer. The serpent’s question, by contrast, already had its verdict built in.

The first chapters of Genesis also lead to a concrete conclusion about the very nature of God. His first words to human beings are a blessing and a gift. There is only one prohibition, and it comes later. This God speaks in order to shape reality and to give life. And He speaks with complete clarity: the one restriction comes with a clear reason, stated plainly and without hedging. The serpent deals in insinuation and things left unsaid. That is the easiest way to tell a word that creates from a word that deceives.

Every day you speak thousands of words: some of them build reality and some of them destroy it. Keeping watch over every one of them would be impossible. But you can pay attention to two key things. First: what hidden assumptions do you smuggle into the questions you ask other people, and into the questions about God you ask yourself in difficult moments? “Does God even remember me?” can be a sincere cry of the heart, but it can also be the serpent’s question, assuming a negative answer from the start. Second, consider how many of your declarations actually create something, such as a promise you intend to keep, or naming out loud the good you see in another person.

Sometimes a small correction is enough, and it costs nothing but a moment’s attention. “You didn’t take out the trash again?” can be turned into a simple statement of fact and a request: “The bag has been sitting there since this morning. Will you take it out before dinner?” The problem to be solved stays exactly the same, but the person you are talking to is not backed into a corner, does not have to defend themselves, and can decide for themselves how to respond.

Language is a tool far more powerful than we usually assume, and the opening pages of the Bible clearly show both of its edges. The most dangerous words turn out to be words about God spoken supposedly in His name. Anyone who uses the argument “God said” only to shame, silence or subdue another person is copying the serpent in Eden: using the Creator’s authority to plant a false picture of Him. That is why in matters of faith it is worth listening very carefully and speaking with great caution, especially when speaking on someone else’s behalf.

questions: What will my words create today?
challenge: **In your thoughts.** Recall one question you asked someone this week that was, at heart, a hidden accusation. In your mind, put together an honest version of it, without the words “again” and “always.”

**In action.** Look through the messages you have sent by phone or email over the last two days. Count the questions that hid a ready-made accusation, and note down who you most often addressed them to. Then take a sheet of paper and write one sentence by hand that will create something good. It might be a promise you will make to someone and intend to keep, or a clear naming of a specific good quality in a friend or someone close to you. Leave the note where the person will find it on their own: in a jacket pocket or between the pages of the book they are reading. If you live alone, simply send it by ordinary mail.
